title: Bengals’ early offensive struggles part of a bigger evolution picture The defense has come out on top most of the time, but OC Dan Pitcher believes rehearsing new looks can pay off. Paul Dehner Jr.

full_text:
Lining up under center is one of the wrinkles Joe Burrow and the Bengals offense have been working on in camp. Andy Lyons / Getty Images
CINCINNATI — The Bengals’ offense looks different through six days of training camp. That’s very much by design.
An offense defined over the years by often-static pre-snap looks and consistently running 11 personnel from shotgun has spent six practices skipping over those basics and advancing directly to exotic wrinkles with under-center motions from every angle imaginable.
“It’s ‘Star Wars’ before the snap,” defensive coordinator Al Golden said.
Indeed, a new hope arrived thanks to the continuity provided by all of last year’s offensive starters returning around Joe Burrow this season. The core plays at the bread and butter of this perennial top-10 offense don’t need months of attention.
Instead, the idea has been to improve underused aspects of the playbook that can make the offense more well-rounded and capable of beating teams in different ways.
Going under center, increasing the use of motions, irregular formations and play action are chief among those play types.
But practicing inconsistent corners of the playbook can lead to inconsistent results. Through six practices, the Bengals’ offense has been just that against the team’s rebuilt defense, which is overwhelmingly winning the days.
Don’t expect panic from the offense, though.
“We feel like this is going to help us build an offense that can win in a number of different ways and one that can win us an AFC North championship,” offensive coordinator Dan Pitcher said. “Whether or not it wins us a training camp trophy, I don’t know, but I don’t really care.”
They may not win trophies, but an award for best visual effects could be in play.
At the center of the unique twists early in camp has been running back Chase Brown, who’s being used all over the formation, similar to the way Ja’Marr Chase has been deployed in recent years. Brown lines up in the slot and runs a slant one play, then takes a jet sweep the next. He’s part of 20 personnel with two running backs, motions into the backfield, behind a fullback and almost any other spot imaginable.
“We all got to prepare a little bit more, at least I do, a lot for the motions and playing F and wherever they are putting me takes a little extra study time because I haven’t really done that before,” Brown said. “It’s cool they trust me doing that and believe in my skill set enough. It’s been fun.”
At one point last weekend, with Brown lined up to the right of Burrow in the shotgun, Chase shifted to the right of Brown. This came not long after a counter run featured a motion, fake and shovel pass to Chase behind it.
The offensive twists are everywhere.
Tight end Drew Sample laughed at the notion that they are showing off an exotic new offense. The longest-tenured Bengal on the roster says this isn’t anything crazy for players to remember, but merely one extra layer on base plays they have run many times.
“We’ve had that play in for eight years,” Sample said of the play with Brown and Chase alongside Burrow in the backfield. “We are just trying different wrinkles with it. That’s the thing to us: We are running the same play, but with some different window dressing. Obviously, with Ja’Marr and Chase Brown we have so many weapons. We have this base play in; how can we really try to f— with them? That’s something that’s really easy for us. We call a slight formation adjustment, but everybody knows it is the same play.”
The pre-snap eye candy and under-center emphasis have helped establish a refreshed run game that the Bengals think will build an encouraging foundation to start the season.
From offensive linemen to defensive and offensive coaches, those around the team have said how impressed they’ve been with how the team looks running downhill out of the under-center offense. Multiple runs broke free for explosive plays Tuesday.
“Guys are being physical,” Pitcher said. “We are building some complementary stuff that is making it hard on the defense. They are making their share of plays, too; that is a formidable group across from us. … It’s coming together.”
The offense has just lacked the excitement and pizazz traditionally associated with its star power.
Safety Bryan Cook, who snagged a pick-6 against Burrow on Monday, was standing in front of his locker after practice and started talking trash to Chase as he walked by, asking him when he will finally catch a deep ball this camp.
The chirping won’t stop until the results come, so the pressure and frustration can mount as so many plays are run into looks that would normally end in check downs, but the offense instead opts to work through the scripted play for the information.
That has resulted in interceptions, defensive playmaking and clunky execution.
It’s all part of the plan, in many ways.
“We are in the process of figuring out who we are going to be as an early-down passing team,” Pitcher said. “There’s going to be some good moments and not-so-good moments when it comes to that.”
That will change soon. The open drive-the-field sessions are coming. Then Burrow and company can pull from any corner of the playbook they want and attack as they see fit. The core of the playbook will be gradually reemphasized as the weeks pass.
For now, the Bengals’ continuity on offense has allowed them to grow beyond the base plays that have made them so great over the years.
The next question becomes, at what point does the offense return to its bread and butter?
“We are also not foolish enough to think we can just snap our fingers and be good at — we have to invest time in whatever we want to be good at,” Pitcher said. “But it’s Aug. 4, and we kick off Sept. 13.”

full_text:
Shedeur Sanders has had two strong throwing days, but the offense has struggled with pre-snap penalties. Nick Cammett / Getty Image
Six practices in, much more is going on at Cleveland Browns training camp than just a quarterback competition. Lots of players are picking off passes. Rookie wide receivers Denzel Boston and KC Concepcion seem big-stage ready. Running back Quinshon Judkins looks healthy. And the remade offensive line is getting challenged every day by a stout defensive front.
A week past the start of full camp and 10 days ahead of the preseason opener, here’s a positional look at what’s been revealed so far and what still needs to be answered as the Browns prepare to move past the installation phase of things and into more competitive situations. (The position groups are listed in order of the author’s confidence in them at this still-early stage.)
Early camp impression: Grant Delpit got the extension he earned with an outstanding 2025. Rookie Emmanuel McNeil-Warren missed most of the spring, but he’s talented and is starting to show up around the ball consistently. Ronnie Hickman is playing for his football future on a restricted free-agent tender and is off to a strong start in camp. Veteran newcomer Daniel Thomas is a physical player who can contribute as a backup and special-teamer, and backup Chris Edmonds has intercepted three passes in six practices.
What’s complicated: With Delpit and Hickman entrenched, the Browns have to figure out McNeil-Warren’s best role. The preseason should help with that since Delpit won’t play much — or at all. The early feeling is the Browns will be in a lot of three-safety looks, but it’s too early to know for sure. It could come down to Thomas versus second-year player Donovan McMillon for the last roster spot, but Edmonds also wants to stick around. Certainly, McNeil-Warren belongs high on any list of players worth watching as August proceeds.
Early camp impression: The pass-rush group has so consistently been in the backfield that nobody’s lamenting the departure of some guy named Myles Garrett — yet. Garrett altered and wrecked opposing game plans, but the Browns only agreed to trade him if they could get Jared Verse in return. Verse has been one of the best players on the practice field and seems to be fitting in nicely. He’s a power-first player and the leader of a group that also includes Alex Wright and Isaiah McGuire, who’s entering the final year of his contract. Verse looks like a keeper, and for now that’s a fine place to start.
What’s complicated: The Browns have been searching for more experience at the position. They flirted with Jadeveon Clowney, who chose the Houston Texans, and in March a reported deal with A.J. Epenesa fell through. The shortage of healthy bodies at defensive tackle probably takes precedence for the personnel department, and in the preseason it’s fair to assume undrafted rookies Logan Fano and Khordae Sydnor will get plenty of chances.
Early camp impression: The Browns drafted two wide receivers last April, and both — Concepcion and Boston — are off to strong starts. Second-year player Isaiah Bond had a strong spring, but he’s had a relatively quiet start to camp. It feels like Jerry Jeudy’s time as the de facto No. 1 wide receiver is coming to an end with Boston looming, but it’s too early to know how things will shake out. Veteran Tylan Wallace will make the roster but will probably be a backup and special teams player primarily.
What’s complicated: In Tuesday’s practice, Concepcion was limited by a shoulder injury he suffered Monday. It probably isn’t a major injury, but the Browns want the 21-year-old to continue to receive reps and opportunities. There likely isn’t room on the roster for holdovers like Cedric Tillman, Jamari Thrash and Gage Larvadain, but the Browns are still evaluating — and hoping their improved depth helps. More than anything, spotty quarterback play makes it hard to evaluate the wide receivers. But this group is definitely improved. These rookies can play.
Early camp impression: The newly extended Denzel Ward remains on top of his game headed into his ninth season and has arguably been the most impressive player in camp. Early concerns about the depth of the cornerback group seem valid, and the Browns signed veteran journeyman Tyler Hall on Tuesday as part of an ongoing effort to add experience.
What’s complicated: With Ward and Tyson Campbell, the Browns have a cornerback duo that’s probably as good as any. But the rest of the group remains unsettled. Myles Harden should again be the top slot cornerback, but nothing past that is clear. Veteran Damarri Mathis was signed last month after he missed all of 2025 with a torn ACL, and if he’s healthy, he can win a roster spot. But Mathis and fellow veteran Myles Bryant were sidelined Tuesday. Cornerback depth is something the Browns could look to address in the coming weeks.
Early camp impression: Judkins seems healthy and explosive. He didn’t have a training camp in his rookie season and spent last winter rehabbing from a significant leg injury, but he seems ahead of schedule and ready for a better season in 2026. He’ll undoubtedly be the workhorse.
What’s complicated: Dylan Sampson will probably play as a third-down back and kickoff returner, and Rocket Sanders is trying to make the 53-man roster as a special teams player and No. 3 running back. Browns coach Todd Monken wants to employ a fullback, too, but it’s too early to know how the offensive personnel will be utilized. Veteran fullback Michael Burton missed last season with an injury and did not participate Tuesday, but he’s expected back soon.
Early camp impression: Four starting spots seem settled, and KT Leveston is battling for the starting right guard spot after starting seven games at tackle last year. Rookie Spencer Fano will be the starting left tackle, but for now he’s alternating days with Dawand Jones. Another rookie, Parker Brailsford, will get some August chances to work with the No. 1 offense, but Elgton Jenkins is the starting center and likely will be when the regular season begins. Monken has been clear that he likes some of what he sees from the group but is open to further experimentation if necessary.
What’s complicated: The Browns know they did a poor job building tackle depth last season, so they’re hoping Jones can stay healthy and give them something. Rookie Austin Barber has worked only at right tackle to this point, but Barber played left tackle in college. Monken thinks Leveston is best at guard, and Teven Jenkins has been absent for several practices, giving Leveston a chance to lock up a starting job. It will be interesting to see how much Monken asks his veterans to play in the preseason for timing purposes and how the Browns choose to protect their competing quarterbacks if none of the veterans play in the preseason games.
Early camp impression: This remains a thin group. Veteran Quincy Williams is off to a strong start, and the Browns need him to be an every-down player. Carson Schwesinger seems on his way to stardom, but the 2025 NFL Defensive Rookie of the Year has missed the last few practices with what the team has called a minor injury. Schwesinger is still working out and probably won’t be sidelined for long, but the Browns are being careful with one of their most gifted players.
What’s complicated: There’s a clear top two, but there’s no proven depth. Young players Easton Mascarenas-Arnold and Winston Reid are taking snaps with the starters, and rookie Justin Jefferson figures to make the roster as a special-teamer and developmental player. Preseason opportunities will be crucial for the construction and evaluation of the rest of the group.

full_text:
Packers tight end Tucker Kraft is working his way back from injury and pointing toward a return in late August. Mike Roemer / Associated Press
GREEN BAY, Wis. — Tucker Kraft exploded from a half-crouch and threw his body into a hit sled with such a thunderous CRACK that a few people standing along the nearby sideline took a half-step back in shock.
“… Psychopath …” a man in the crowd said softly, awed. Kraft repositioned the sled and lined up again. CRACK .
The Green Bay Packers tight end, a blossoming superstar and now among the NFL’s elite at the position, can’t do everything he wants in practice just yet. He continues to work his way back to full participation after tearing his ACL in a Week 9 game in November.
Head coach Matt LaFleur said Sunday that Kraft could realistically get the green light for joint practices in late August with the Arizona Cardinals. Until then, his on-field work will incrementally increase from what it was during my three-day visit to Packers camp this week: a number of short catch-and-run plays in individual drills, straight-line ball-carrier drills with the running backs, some blocking drills with the hit pads and not against live competition and other similar exercises. By the time those practices roll around, Kraft may even have a new contract — he is due for a massive extension, although he has said he’ll play his fourth NFL season without it if it comes to that — and this ongoing negotiation is quietly in the background of Kraft’s eventual return to the field as a player through whom much of the Packers offense will flow.
There was a sense before his injury that Kraft was only picking up steam; with that came a certain edge for a Packers team that, though always very good and always with a high ceiling, simply has not been able to get past the divisional round over the last five seasons. Kraft was giving sharper teeth to a very good team in a town that so beautifully immortalizes great .
In 2026, that very good team needs its stars to be great — healthy, and great.
Monday, what mattered was that Kraft and his teammates put pads on for the first time. And even though he would be limited in the day’s practice, he wanted to freaking hit something.
CRACK . The force of Kraft’s attack on the sled reminded me of a specific play he and LaFleur love to run — and did often in 2025, when the Packers were the No. 2 offense in EPA per play between Weeks 1 and 8. It is a play that can be either a run or pass concept depending on how the defense aligns to its pre-snap look, but is supposed to present as a duo run — especially if that defense is playing in shell coverage (two safeties up high). At the snap, Kraft and his blocking assignment — usually a defensive end — crash into each other at full force to help sell the play as a run right as quarterback Jordan Love executes a play-action fake, then Kraft shakes off the defender and bolts up and across the field where Love zips him the ball.
“I’m gonna come off the line of scrimmage and I’m gonna strike this guy as hard as I can. Then I’m gonna get lost. (It’s) a dead sprint to the sideline,” Kraft said. “(And) … the job after that is to catch the ball and make them pay.”
Kraft said that most defenses know the Packers will run this play. But, he noted with a grin, it still works; an embodiment of the “f— you energy” that seems to run through the otherwise low-key Kraft’s blood every time he takes the field.
“The moment the ball hits my hands, it’s on. I’m trying to squeeze every inch out of every play,” he said. “… I want the entire defense to come and try to tackle me. You just put that stress on ’em. They’re gonna have to run down 85.”
With the ball in his hands, Kraft is more boulder-from-“Raiders of the Lost Ark” than he is human. “I guess people don’t really want to tackle him,” LaFleur joked. Before Kraft got hurt, he had the highest yards-after-catch per reception of any non-running back in the NFL (11.2), which also was fifth-highest overall.
“That mindset that not one person is gonna bring him down; not one person can guard him … he makes it come to life in the games,” Love told me. “It’s definitely that ‘f— you’ mindset, ‘I’m better than you.’ That dog mentality. You love guys that have that. It’s an edge, for sure.”
Spending time in Green Bay is a powerful type of magic for any football fan. Driving from the airport into Titletown at night means following the glow of the Lambeau Field signage lofted high overhead — the classic, specifically green stadium itself dwarfing the homes around it and shedding soft light across those with front yards that eagerly face it from across the street. Many of those yards feature fences that are painted with tributes to players past and present; street names are “Holmgren Way” and “Lombardi Ave.” and “Brett Favre Pass.” Packers fans, please excuse this breathless tourism about a holy land you all know so well. Even the wildflowers growing in the street medians around the stadium are yellow and green. Come on .
Yet magic and a high floor have lately only gotten this version of the Packers so far into the postseason. Perhaps understanding this, the organization was uncharacteristically aggressive in acquiring top pass rusher Micah Parsons via trade last summer. It was a sign, to me, that the front office knew it had to swing harder for the kind of math-changing talent that truly gives teams an advantage when the playoffs begin and game plans become more matchup-focused by the week. Other teams — the Los Angeles Rams, to name one Super Bowl-winning example — previously showed what is possible for a very good team when it pushes its chips in for elite players. More — the Cincinnati Bengals, Denver Broncos and San Francisco 49ers — have followed a similar model in recent seasons; the Rams also just did, again . Yet that gamble is perilous, sometimes expensive and sometimes doesn’t even pay off. How fortuitous for the Packers, then, that they didn’t just bring in Parsons but had a couple of elite home-grown players, too, in the explosive, punishing Kraft and the serene, exceptional Love.
It doesn’t always work out. Optimism at the start of last season was so high, and then Parsons and Kraft got hurt, Love played through a couple of dings and dents of his own and Green Bay suffered a second consecutive exit in the wild-card round. Most NFL teams would love to have this problem. The Packers — and their loyal fans — want more.
Kraft seems to understand the line the franchise is trying to walk between its storied foundation and thirst to go bolder with its future. Intermixed between bone-rattling hits, unpoetic fundamentals and ground-out yards-after-the-catch, Kraft is a self-described “nuisance” to opponents and a total showman for his teammates and fans.
“One thing we say around here is ‘if you’re juiceless, you’re useless,’” he said. “If you don’t have the confidence, exuberance to go out there and put your show on, then what are you really doing?”
Last week, local reporters captured video of Kraft running a lap around the field before practice began, pumping his fist toward the applauding crowd. A couple teammates pumped their own fists. Maybe they couldn’t help it. Kraft says he wants to be a “thermostat” for the team this year. As he gets healthier and recaptures his rising star, I believe he will be.
• In my mind, there is a pre-Parsons-return defense, and a post-Parsons-return defense.
The former may have to depend more heavily on scheme, manufactured pressure and other designed twists to give depth and question-mark areas a lift, while the latter could still feature all of that — plus many initial questions and concerns will ultimately be solved with Parsons on the field.

title: The Texans have the pieces; can C.J. Stroud finally get Houston over the hump? Stroud doesn't need to carry the Texans — the defense can do that. Houston just needs precision and sound decision-making from its QB. Mike Jones 1
summary: The Texans have the pieces; can C.J. Stroud finally get Houston over the hump? Stroud doesn't need to carry the Texans — the defense can do that. Houston just needs precision and sound decision-making from its QB. Mike Jones
full_text:
The Texans have a championship-caliber defense. Can C.J. Stroud become the elite decision-maker Houston needs to contend? Alex Slitz / Getty Images
HOUSTON — An exasperated C.J. Stroud steps back from his center and claps his hands emphatically to punctuate an admonishment to multiple members of his revamped offensive line.
They had fallen for their own Houston Texans quarterback ’s hard count, aborting a play midway through an 11-on-11 series on Day 4 of training camp. Stroud and company quickly reset, with the fourth-year pro barking another cadence. This time, the play gets off without a hitch. Stroud takes a quick drop, turns to his right and hits Nico Collins in stride on a slant, allowing the powerful wide receiver to deliver a chain-moving gain. Stroud’s body language conveys a “that’s more like it” attitude as the players stride to the new line of scrimmage.
They’re entrenched in the dog days of summer with the start of the 2026 NFL season still more than a month away. The Texans have lofty expectations; coach DeMeco Ryans and his assistants have made precision a point of emphasis during camp. Regardless of position, the Texans must be precise — with positioning, hand and foot placement, assignment execution and certainly snap counts. The devil’s in the details, as they say, and the Texans can ill afford to derail another potential-rich season by committing self-inflicted mistakes.
This is a crucial year for the Texans, who have failed in three straight attempts to get over the divisional playoff round hump . Still, few individuals find themselves under the pressure that rests on Stroud’s shoulders.
A symbol of hope when Houston drafted him with the No. 2 pick in 2023, and one of the catalysts for three straight postseason appearances, Stroud fell prey to uncharacteristically poor ball security last winter. Those decision-making errors and execution lapses cost the Texans a trip to the Super Bowl. Given the dominant nature of their defense during the playoffs, Houston could have cruised to Santa Clara had Stroud avoided the four interceptions (panic-induced throws he had no business forcing) that cost the Texans dearly against the eventual AFC representative New England Patriots.
Even after Stroud’s dreadful performance against the Patriots, Ryans profusely expressed support for and undying loyalty to his quarterback. Then, during the offseason, Texans general manager Nick Caserio did everything in his power to upgrade Stroud’s supporting cast. He further fortified an already imposing defense and overhauled the Texans’ offensive line, tight end and running back position groups.
Caserio did not, however, award Stroud a record-breaking long-term contract extension, opting instead to take a patient approach by letting the passer play out the fourth season of his rookie deal before revisiting the contract.
Anchoring the team is a star-studded defense featuring one of the best pass-rushing tandems — Will Anderson Jr. and Danielle Hunter — physical, rangy middle linebacker Azeez Al-Shaair, impressive defensive backs Derek Stingley Jr., Kamari Lassiter and Calen Bullock and free-agent pickup Reed Blankenship.
To upgrade a pass-catching unit highlighted by Collins, Tank Dell and emerging options Jayden Higgins and Jaylin Noel, Caserio drafted tight end Marlin Klein in the second round and signed veteran Foster Moreau to complement Dalton Schultz. He traded for David Montgomery, pairing the punishing, downhill runner with young Woody Marks to form a versatile backfield. Caserio also drafted center Keylan Rutledge in the first round out of Georgia Tech, signed three-time Pro Bowl guard Wyatt Teller to line up alongside promising second-year left tackle Aireontae Ersery and added eight-year veteran Braden Smith as insurance for massive right tackle Trent Brown.
Now, Stroud must do his part and provide the leadership, poise and execution necessary to turn this promising roster into a true juggernaut.
Confidence, comfort and decision-making are the key areas the Texans hope and need to see Stroud grow the most. His coaches and teammates believe the quarterback is capable of doing so.
One of the elements that made Stroud’s rookie season so impressive involved his passing accuracy and ability to take care of the football. That 2023 season saw him complete 63.9 percent of his passes while throwing 23 touchdowns and only five interceptions. While Stroud regressed in Year 2, throwing 12 interceptions along with 20 touchdowns, he took steps toward improvement last season — his first with current offensive coordinator Nick Caley — and posted a career-best completion percentage (64.5) and cut down on his turnovers (eight interceptions) while throwing 19 touchdown passes.
Last winter’s playoff struggles left a lasting impression, but Caley says Stroud displayed significant growth last season and sees signs of further improvement this season based on Stroud’s greater understanding of the system.
“You see it just in his confidence,” Caley said after Friday’s practice. “Comfort level, just his process. He’s very steady. He can move on from one play to the next, sees the game very well. He has just put in a lot of time, man. But I just see the Year 2 step in the system, and I’m proud of him. And, it’s not just C.J., but the entire offense — the guys that are back from last year. You can feel it just even in terms of the operation, in terms of understanding fully — the ins and the outs, the 300 and 400 levels of everything that we’re doing now.”
Said Bullock, “You can see C.J.’s more comfortable out there based on him making better reads, quicker decisions with the ball. He’s our leader, but he will ask us questions about things we see, and he’ll tell us what he’s seeing.”
As they observe Stroud’s approach to mastering the Texans’ system, sharpening his skills and cultivating relationships within the locker room, teammates have drawn inspiration from Stroud.
“He just does everything the right way,” Ersery declared. “And as somebody I care about, I want to protect and make sure he’s got a good clean pocket when he goes out there so he doesn’t have to overthink or anything like that; just so he can play fast and play his game.”
Said Teller, “He is absolutely one of the most genuine, caring young men I know. Intelligent. First day we were talking ball, and I was just like, ‘Whoa, you know ball.’ I’ve spent a lot of time in this league and there’s things that I’m learning still, and there’s things that I know pretty dang well, and it shows you how intelligent he is when he’s teaching you something, and you’re six years older than him.”
When it comes to supporting Stroud, Houston’s defense has already done a strong job, holding foes to 277.2 yards (fewest in the NFL) and 17.4 points (second-fewest) while racking up 29 takeaways (third-most). Meanwhile, Caley believes moves made this offseason will also lead to an improved rushing attack. That should translate into more success on first and second downs, more manageable third-down situations and from there, Stroud must capitalize — and not in some dramatic way.
When discussing areas of needed growth for Stroud and the passing attack, Ryans revealed a specific challenge he extended.
“One thing I’ve been harping on with our quarterbacks is just, ‘Let’s be elite decision makers. You touch the football every single snap. So as the quarterback, you have to make great decisions with the football, and sometimes a great decision, it may not be throwing the football, it may be tucking it, it may be running it. It may be throwing the ball in the dirt. But just make great decisions, and know we always have that next-play mentality.’”
Because of the stature of their position, quarterbacks often feel the pressure to deliver great heroics. But if he takes Ryans’ words to heart, the simplistic approach of mastering the details, focusing on precision and sound decision-making, Stroud could give himself his best chance of fully delivering…

full_text:
Will Kyler Murray win the Vikings QB competition over J.J. McCarthy? David Berding / Getty Images
EAGAN, Minn. — Kyler Murray and J.J. McCarthy aren’t just competing to become the Minnesota Vikings’ starting quarterback . The winner of that duel will claim a premium opportunity to revitalize their career and potentially even thrive under coach Kevin O’Connell’s tutelage.
The Vikings also have plenty at stake, with McCarthy’s first-round trajectory stunted by injuries, and Murray offering a tantalizing amount of athleticism and raw talent. Collectively, the Vikings again have enough firepower to distinguish themselves as playoff contenders if they can get more from their QB. They won 27 games over the two seasons (2022, 2024) under O’Connell when their No. 1 quarterback suited up for every game, but they started four QBs in 2023, three in 2025, and, unsurprisingly, missed the postseason each time.
With the Vikings donning pads this week in training camp, this has been viewed as the first potential checkpoint where Murray could separate himself from his young competitor. Murray’s experience and ability to make plays in a variety of ways, particularly as Vikings defensive coordinator Brian Flores attempts to rain hell on his offensive coworkers, figure to give him an advantage over McCarthy in practice.
Murray, the No. 1 pick in 2019, showed flashes of tantalizing potential during eight seasons with the Arizona Cardinals. At his best earlier in his career, the 2019 NFL Rookie of the Year was proficient enough to earn a pair of Pro-Bowl nods and even a place in the early-season MVP discussion. But too often, late-season swoons, injury woes and organizational disarray thwarted what might have been.
Murray has a polarizing reputation around the NFL . While his talent is undeniable — and the Vikings are already gushing about his athleticism — he has not always been the most popular teammate.
Now for the first time, there might be a chicken-or-egg resolution. Had this been more of a Murray issue or a Cardinals problem?
For instance, by all accounts, Murray has been well received by his new Vikings teammates. O’Connell’s culture and the locker room’s leadership have been well established, and four years of NFLPA report cards have told the story of two organizations with very different standings around the league. The Vikings have finished first or second in the grading in all four of O’Connell’s seasons, while the Cardinals’ average ranking has been 30.3, including three years in the bottom two.
While there are varying reasons for the Cardinals’ consistently low rankings, there’s little doubt Murray’s last four seasons in Arizona were tumultuous, both organizationally and due to his own poor injury luck. His head coach, Kliff Kingsbury, was fired after the 2022 season, and the team brought in head coach Jonathan Gannon and offensive coordinator Drew Petzing to lead a rebuild, which clouded Murray’s standing with the team. Arizona opted to stick with Murray, who was coming off a late-season ACL tear, as the QB tried to acclimate to a new offense after rejoining the team in November. He started eight games in 2023 with mild success (89.4 passer rating) before returning in 2024 to play a full slate of games for the first time since 2020.
Of course, Murray, who turns 29 on Friday, couldn’t stay on the field last year, as a foot injury limited him to just five games. Murray has missed 30 games since 2021, so he’s far from a finished product. He proved in 2024 that he can start 17 games, but Murray must now show he can produce at a higher level when the injuries mount. And with a shorter frame and scrambling play style, the injury threat isn’t going to disappear with a new mailing address.
However, if Murray can flourish, he could enter 2027 as the prized QB in free agency, or he would at least be a strong candidate for an extension or franchise tag. O’Connell has already helped Kirk Cousins, Sam Darnold and, to a lesser extent, Daniel Jones rebuild their value and pad their bank accounts with big paydays from new organizations. Murray could be next, though the Vikings, for their part, might be tiring of preparing a new veteran each offseason and could try to keep Murray.
But if Murray walks in 2027, the Vikings will have options — like they always do. There’s a reason Murray and every notable QB on the market wanted to join the Vikings last offseason. O’Connell’s reputation as a quarterback savant has grown with each season, to the point that it’s becoming more common to hear prominent decision-makers in other buildings refer to him as one of the five best coaches in the league. If the Vikings are going to keep the assembly line moving, there will be plenty of veteran QBs eager to get in line to work with O’Connell.
That’s, of course, if McCarthy isn’t able to take the reins.
McCarthy, a 2024 first-round pick, should have a better understanding of O’Connell’s system in Year 3, but his lack of game experience could be tough to overcome in a race against Murray. McCarthy lost his rookie season because of meniscus surgery, and he won the starting job last year in training camp before missing time in the regular season with a high ankle sprain, concussion and a hairline fracture in his throwing hand.
McCarthy has struggled in his first 10 NFL starts, but that’s not exactly rare for a young quarterback. However, exacerbating the issue, he’s never made more than four starts in a row, as McCarthy’s injuries have wiped away any chance to establish consistency. Just like Murray, it’s up to McCarthy to prove he can remain healthy.
All things being equal, O’Connell is going to start the quarterback who gives the Vikings the best chance to win this season. But health can’t be discounted. Murray, who has made 14 starts in November over eight seasons, has been vulnerable to injuries as seasons have progressed.
McCarthy must remain ready if he doesn’t win the job out of camp because of Murray’s injury history. And there are several quarterbacks who have carved out successful careers after quiet starts, so it’ll be paramount for McCarthy to maximize his time to learn if he doesn’t beat out Murray.
But that’s a discussion for another time. Now at least, there’s still a job to win, and the stakes are high enough that career trajectories might be on the line.

title: Thoughts on the Patriots’ 44 defensive players a week into training camp We break down every player on the New England defense, a unit that has looked solid thus far in training camp. Chad Graff 1
summary:
Mike Vrabel is hoping the Patriots defense can be as good as it was last season, when the team rode the unit to a Super Bowl appearance. Eric Canha / Imagn Images
The New England Patriots defense got the better of the offense during Tuesday’s training camp practice, mostly shutting down the run and limiting big plays in the passing game.
That makes this the perfect time to offer a quick thought on every defensive player on the Patriots, one day after looking at the offense .
Harold Landry, edge:
full_text:
Mike Vrabel is hoping the Patriots defense can be as good as it was last season, when the team rode the unit to a Super Bowl appearance. Eric Canha / Imagn Images
The New England Patriots defense got the better of the offense during Tuesday’s training camp practice, mostly shutting down the run and limiting big plays in the passing game.
That makes this the perfect time to offer a quick thought on every defensive player on the Patriots, one day after looking at the offense .
Harold Landry, edge: A disappointing offseason for the veteran, whose lingering injury has kept him out of practice. When healthy, he’s been really good for the Pats. But health is a real question as Week 1 nears. And this is not a position where there is a great deal of depth.
Milton Williams, DT: I thought it was a risk a year ago to give a guy who had never played more than 50 percent of his team’s snaps in a season so much money. I was dead wrong. Williams has been everything you’d want and looks primed for another strong year.
Christian Barmore, DT: The team has managed his workload and worked with him on converting pressures into sacks after notching just two a year ago. The guess here is he triples that number this season.
Dre’Mont Jones, edge: His size stands out (6-3, 268), and he should help against the run. The question is whether he can contribute enough as a pass rusher in his eighth year in the league.
Cory Durden, DL: Last season was easily the most productive of his career, and now he has a chance to build on that after the team didn’t re-sign Khyiris Tonga.
Joshua Farmer, DL: It’s not often fourth-round picks are cut 18 months after being drafted, but Farmer is on the roster bubble entering preseason games.
Eric Gregory, DL: He brings size (6-3, 319) to the interior that the team otherwise lacks, and while run defense is his calling card, he’ll need to show that in the preseason to earn a spot.
Leonard Taylor, DL: His length is noticeable on the interior (and contributed to his field goal block in the AFC Championship Game), where he can gain space from would-be blockers.
Jeremiah Pharms, DL: It speaks to his ability to do his job that Pharms has stuck on the Patriots’ roster the past three years through three different coaches as an undrafted player out of Friends University.
David Blay Jr., DL: He’s undersized at 6-2 and 292 pounds and lacks explosiveness, but a path to the practice squad is within reach.
Isaiah Iton, DL: He went undrafted in 2024 but has pass-rush upside the Pats hope to develop.
Casey Rogers, DL: The Pats added him to the roster this week, and he brings an elite athletic profile after running a 4.86 time in the 40-yard dash and leaping 35 inches at 294 pounds.
Gabe Jacas, edge: His early summer absence has resulted in some friendly ribbing, with coach Mike Vrabel forcing him to the front of the room to present to the group during team meetings. Jacas spoke Tuesday for the first time since signing but declined to get into when he underwent the knee surgery that prolonged his negotiations, only saying that he feels good following the procedure.
Elijah Ponder, edge: Praise continues to pour in for the undrafted second-year player, but translating that to in-game success is the next step.
Bradyn Swinson, edge: He dropped 15 pounds and looks noticeably faster, and the Patriots really need a rusher like Swinson to earn a spot in the rotation.
Quintayvious Hutchins, edge: Size isn’t his strength at 6-3, 245 pounds, so he needs to win with speed. He could still push for a roster spot with a strong preseason.
Jesse Luketa, edge: After three years with the Cardinals, he spent most of last season on the Rams’ practice squad.
Xavier Holmes, edge: He made the 90-man roster after impressing at a rookie minicamp tryout, but his most likely path is the practice squad.
Robert Spillane, LB: No word yet on any additional strange workouts added to his offseason routine, but Spillane remains an elite run stuffer and has made life difficult in camp for Rhamondre Stevenson and TreVeyon Henderson.
Christian Elliss, LB: The Pats have a little more linebacker depth this year, so Elliss will need to do his part against the pass to keep his starting job.
Chad Muma, LB: He’s the linebacker whose stock is most on the rise, playing with the starters in base defense on Tuesday.
KJ Britt, LB: The free-agent signing hasn’t looked head and shoulders ahead of the rest of the backups, which you’d hope for from a five-year vet.
Namdi Obiazor, LB: Special teams will be important to his path to a roster spot, but he said Tuesday that’s a role he wants to take on. Still, his chances likely bank on the team keeping five linebackers, which is not a given.
Amari Gainer, LB: Speed and athleticism are his calling cards, but he’ll need to use them on special teams to earn a spot.
Riley Wilson, LB: His speed shows up on kickoff coverage, but the Patriots are going to have to be picky with which linebackers they keep, considering they may want six cornerbacks on the roster.
Khalil Jacobs, LB: The former Missouri Tiger was a late add to the undrafted rookie class in May and has mostly been with the third-team defense.
Christian Gonzalez, CB: Even amid a lengthy contract negotiation , Gonzalez has played physical football and looked every bit like the No. 1 cornerback. It wouldn’t be a surprise if, at the end of 2026, he’s viewed as the best corner in the league.
Carlton Davis, CB: Injuries have lingered, keeping him out of recent practices. The skill set is there, but he’ll turn 30 this season. Depth at outside corner is a question, so the Pats need him to get — and stay — healthy.
Marcus Jones, CB: He’s incredible in coverage as a nickel corner, but there are concerns given his size (5-8, 188) and how much he can contribute in run defense. The team has toyed with the idea of a big nickel defense where they swap a safety in for Jones in potential running situations.
Karon Prunty, CB: His stock continues to rise as the fifth-round rookie gets more and more opportunities and keeps making the most of them. If this continues, he could be the No. 3 outside corner.
Charles Woods, CB: Versatility always helps make a case for a roster spot, and Woods has shown he can back up Jones in the slot or Davis on the outside.
Kobee Minor, CB: Maybe it’s because he has drawn some tough matchups against top receivers, or maybe it’s been because of mistakes elsewhere that he’s trying to cover up, but Minor just seems to get beaten a lot in practice.
Kindle Vildor, CB: A lack of length hurts him on the outside, but the veteran of 80 NFL games has stuck around for a reason.
Channing Canada, CB: Tuesday wasn’t his best practice, but he has the speed to run with the Patriots’ top receivers, which has shown up on deep balls.
Marcellas Dial, CB: Special teams is his calling card, but it looks like he’s on the wrong side of the roster bubble.
Kenneth Harris, CB: He’s a great athlete (he posted a 39.5-inch vertical leap) but needs more development to play at this level.
Brandon Crossley, CB: He’s a roster long shot who could use a strong preseason.
Kevin Byard, S: He has quickly become one of the leaders on defense, and his ball skills stand out, which is why he tends to rack up so many interceptions.
Craig Woodson, S: A breakout season could be on the horizon for Woodson, who has been excellent this summer and should form a great safety duo with Byard. The back end of the defense is much stronger than the front.
Dell Pettus, S: A hard hitter even in practice, Pettus has improved his ball skills with help, he said, from Byard.
John Saunders, S: The Pats want to use a third safety in some big nickel packages, so look for Saunders to get a chance there against the Colts next week.
Mike Brown, S: He brings experience to the back end of the defense after playing nine games last season, but that spot is such a strength that it’s not clear Brown makes the team.
Brenden Schooler, S: An undisclosed injury has kept Schooler…

full_text:
The Giants are hoping for big seasons from rookies (left to right) Arvell Reese, Colton Hood, Malachi Fields and Francis Mauigoa. John Jones / Imagn Images
WHITE SULPHUR SPRINGS, W.Va. — Linebacker Arvell Reese likes to describe himself as a physical and fast player. A week into training camp, the New York Giants’ top pick of the 2026 draft class has looked the part.
Reese has been starting at inside linebacker alongside Tremaine Edmunds, who was brought in during free agency. While there was some pre-draft chatter around the league about pushing Reese outside and letting him use his quick first step off the edge, the Giants were clear from the start that the rookie would be playing inside.
It’s early, but the decision to keep him at linebacker looks to have been a wise one. During the first week of camp, Reese put his speed and IQ on display, most memorably when he got himself in position to bat down a pass in zone coverage. Reese’s acumen caught the eye of coach John Harbaugh, who later called it a “great football play.”
In Week 2 of camp, with the pads finally on, the 6-foot-4, 243-pound Reese has shown off his other trait the Giants love so much: his physicality. My beat partner, Dan Duggan, documented on Monday how Reese was consistently blowing up plays in the offensive backfield, paving the way for his veteran teammates to rave about him afterwards.
“I think he’s going to be a pretty dang good player,” right tackle Jermaine Eluemunor said. “I’m glad he’s on our team. I’ll tell you that. He’s quick, he’s physical. You can tell he truly loves this game and that his instincts are just ridiculous. I had one play today where I climbed to the second level, and we smacked each other, and I tripped, just in case there’s a video (laughter). I got tripped. I got tripped! There was something behind me, and I got table-topped! … I like him a lot.”
Reese, who spoke with The Athletic before Monday’s first padded practice, wasn’t trying to get ahead of himself. Instead, the mild-mannered rookie classified his play as “all right,” saying there’s always room for improvement. He said his early focus during film breakdowns with inside linebackers coach Frank Bush and defensive coordinator Dennard Wilson is his approach in pass coverage.
“I know it’ll get better as I get more reps and watch more film,” Reese said. “But just understanding route concepts and not just dropping back and just waiting for something to happen. You know, jumping routes; I want to be more active in coverage.”
While the Giants are focused on improving Reese’s abilities as an inside linebacker, they will still let him loose off the edge every so often, especially if he keeps on beating an All-Pro like Andrew Thomas for sacks, as he did on Monday.
“He’s been playing well the whole camp since he got here,” Harbaugh said Monday. “You see the talent, obviously. I think he’s very sharp for a first-year guy. He gets things right pretty much all the time, makes very few mistakes. He’s a very serious-minded guy, and he’s very determined.”
Reese has been an early standout, but how are some of the other rookies faring as the second week of camp continues?
The Giants’ No. 10 pick has slotted in at right guard alongside four returning starters: Thomas at left tackle, Jon Runyan Jr. at left guard, John Michael Schmitz at center and Eluemunor at right tackle.
While it’s challenging to paint the picture of how a lineman is faring until after the pads are on, Harbaugh has been impressed with what he’s seen so far. The same goes for his teammates on both sides of the ball.
“I like playing next to him,” Eluemunor said Monday. “He holds everyone accountable. You can tell he has that leadership trait that is rare in a young guy his age. … The sky’s the limit for him, too. I think him and Arvell are going to be huge players for us this year.”
While Eluemunor likes playing next to him, the Giants hope defensive linemen will hate playing across from him. He’ll need to establish that kind of reputation for himself during the regular season, but he’s already creating some buzz along the Giants’ defensive line.
“He’s very heavy-handed, and he can move,” veteran defensive tackle DJ Reader said. “It’s good to be around some young, joyful energy. I’m getting up there in some years. He’s a kid; I know he’s going to make me bring it every day. He’s going to make me better for it, and he’s going to get better for it. … I’ve enjoyed our little battles back and forth. We’ve been having a good time.”
A durable blocker whose best NFL role may be as a guard rather than right tackle.
Reader added that Mauigoa is fun to be around off the field; fans got a little taste of that when Mauigoa was the designated rookie tasked with running around the field to hype up the crowd before practice .
“He definitely has confidence,” Thomas said. “You can see it on the field, just the energy he plays with and just going out there attacking, the effort that he plays with. … A lot of times, you come out here, you’re thinking a lot when you’re a rookie just trying to understand the speed. But you can see him flying off the ball; he’s excited to get after it.”
The battle for the No. 2 cornerback job is one of the most interesting and consequential position battles of camp. Hood has been a big part of that competition, just as Harbaugh said he would be after the team selected him in the second round. Paulson Adebo and Greg Newsome entered the summer as the two top corners on the depth chart, and they’ve stayed in those roles so far, but Hood and 2023 first-rounder Deonte Banks have played first-team reps and look impressive.
While Hood committed two penalties in coverage in Monday’s first padded practice, he also recorded an interception in one of last week’s end-of-game situations, which he returned for a touchdown. Though a penalty negated the play, it was impressive.
Hood may have a chance to endear himself to coaches once the preseason begins. One of the very first things GM Joe Schoen said about Hood after they drafted him in May was that he isn’t “afraid to throw his body around and tackle. He’s physical and truly loves ball.”
“I want a bunch of pit bulls out there flying around making plays on the football,” Harbaugh added. “And Colton Hood gives us another guy in there to do that and compete and push everybody.”
A balanced, scrappy athlete who can attach himself to receivers; likely an early starter.
Fields’ standout play this camp came Saturday as the Giants started their team period. Fields reeled in a deep sideline pass from quarterback Jaxson Dart (thrown with Abdul Carter in his face) despite solid coverage from Newsome.
The further we’ve gotten into camp, the better the third-round pick has looked as a deep target for Dart.
To be clear, Fields is getting a lot of work with Dart and the starters. During Saturday’s end-of-practice situational period, when the offense was down 11 points with 6:24 left, Dart targeted Fields twice for completions.
“He’s been great,” Adebo said of Fields. “I think he’s quick. He’s a big receiver, but he also has some speed to him as well, so he reminds me of, kind of those old school, traditional, like (former NFL wide receiver) Terrell Owens-type receiver who can go up and get the ball but also has the speed to kind of break away from you, if need be, so he’s been great this whole offseason.”
Fields and veteran Darius Slayton could be in line to compete for some deep targets once the season gets going. With tight end Isaiah Likely patrolling the intermediate area of the field and Malik Nabers doing a bit of everything, the Giants need field-stretchers. Fields looks like he could fit the bill.

— New York Giants (@Giants) August 3, 2026
The sixth-rounder has quietly put together a strong start to camp and finds himself around the ball when lining up alongside inside linebacker Micah McFadden with the second-team defense. On Saturday, he helped break up a pass…

full_text:
Acquired in a trade with Miami, Minkah Fitzpatrick could be exactly what the Jets need in the secondary. Seth Wenig / Associated Press
FLORHAM PARK, N.J. — The New York Jets are into their second week of training camp. There will be no (or shouldn’t be any) sweeping conclusions made based on what has transpired so far, but there is plenty to be learned.
A few players — some expected, some surprises — have stood out through five practices, two of them in pads. Here’s a look at eight who have caught my eye:
An argument could be made Membou has been the best player on the field in training camp. He’s at least been the best player on offense. Membou has been dominant at times, especially since Monday when the pads came on. There was one practice last week during which David Bailey got the better of him on a few reps, but that hasn’t happened much since.
On Tuesday, Membou didn’t let any pass rushers near Geno Smith and opened up holes in the running game. During one-on-one drills, Will McDonald tried using his agility and speed to get around him, but Membou blocked him all the way around the pocket and then into the ground. Bailey attempted to bull rush him, and it didn’t go anywhere. Membou looked like a high-caliber tackle as a rookie, and he appears ready to make a leap in Year 2.
“I just knew that he was going to come back in the offseason program and just be stone-faced and ready to go,” Jets coach Aaron Glenn said. “And he was exactly that. Man, he has this look on his face right now to where every rep matters, every rep counts. … He’s operating at a high level right now.”
His battles with Bailey have been fun to watch.
“He’s a really good player, man,” Bailey said. “Good feet, good low center of gravity, and he’s ridiculously strong. He’s been getting me better.”
Membou has been the Jets’ best player on offense, and on defense, it’s probably been Fitzpatrick. The Jets haven’t had this caliber of safety since Jamal Adams and Marcus Maye were at their best in 2019. Maybe Fitzpatrick isn’t the same player he was in his prime, but he’s quickly made an impact on the back end, much needed for a group of defensive backs that put together one of the worst statistical seasons in team history last season.
Fitzpatrick has had either an interception or close to one in just about every practice, including a pick off Smith on the first play of team drills Monday. He always seems to be in the right place, and Glenn is using him all over the formation. His teammates and coaches have raved about the impact he’s made behind the scenes, too.
Last week, Bailey had about as dominant a practice as you’ll see out of a rookie pass rusher, getting two or three “sacks” (there is no contact on the quarterback in practice) and a couple of tackles for loss. He hasn’t reached quite that peak since, but he’s still looked far and away like the Jets’ best edge rusher through five practices.
He’s had more success going against left tackle Olu Fashanu than Membou on the offense’s right side.
“He’s been a pain, man,” Membou said. “He’s a great player. He’s smooth, he’s quick, and he’s got a natural ability to rush the passer.”
Bailey’s get-off and burst is his best and most obvious trait, but his strength in bull rushes has been impressive. He’s made an impact in the running game, too, a significant development considering that was a big question for him coming into the NFL. The Jets will rotate their edge rushers, but Bailey has been getting most of the reps with Joe Ossai injured. Kingsley Enagbare was stepped on during Monday’s practice and sat out Tuesday.
“I’m just having fun with my brothers out there,” Bailey said.
Maybe this is a product of watching Justin Fields practice last year — and Zach Wilson in years past — but it has been a welcome sight to watch a quarterback who, at the very least, can make all the throws and is willing to try them. He was perfect in Saturday’s practice (11 for 11 in 11-on-11 drills), though Smith came back down to earth Monday, throwing an interception on his first pass attempt. (Monday’s practice was affected by pouring rain.)
Smith was far from perfect Tuesday — 7 of 12 with an interception in 11-on-11 — but that doesn’t accurately highlight the quality of some plays he made in team drills. The interception was a poor throw into traffic, deflected by Jamien Sherwood into the arms of cornerback Brandon Stephens. Then Smith nearly threw another pick a couple of plays later, but otherwise, he was mostly on the money.
On one play, he stood strong in the pocket as pressure came and threw a laser across his body into a tight window, complete to tight end Mason Taylor. Later, he connected with Garrett Wilson down the sideline on a perfect throw, hauled in by a toe-tapping Wilson for a 15-20 yard completion. He later connected with wide receiver Isaiah Williams on another deep ball, 20-25 yards down the field.
There’s something to be said about a quarterback who 1. can make all the throws, 2. isn’t afraid to take risks and 3. doesn’t let a mistake (such as an interception) affect him afterward.
Rookie Cade Klubnik is also worth mentioning: He’s completed 10 of 16 passes in two padded practices and appears to have a real command of the offense. He’s doing a solid job of reading the defense and making quick decisions. Preseason will go a long way toward figuring out whether he’s ready to be QB2.
It felt like Nahshon Wright had the edge in the spring, but through five practices, it feels like Thomas is more likely to emerge as the starter opposite Brandon Stephens. He held up well against Wilson in Tuesday’s practice, nearly intercepting Smith at one point. Glenn has been tough on him — when he was asked how Thomas was playing last week, Glenn said he’d wait to answer that until he saw him in pads.
On Tuesday, Glenn said Thomas was “doing well” but that he still needed to shake off some rust.
Thomas started five games last season, then suffered a season-ending injury, missing out on valuable experience. He said last year he “hesitated” a lot, so he focused this offseason on “trusting my eyes.”
“There were a lot of plays I left out there” in 2025, he said.
T’Vondre Sweat (hamstring) remains out, which has given Jackson a real opportunity to push for playing time. The fourth-round rookie is making the most of it so far. His size (6 feet 5, 315) is unique for a nose tackle, and he’s made his mark even against Jets interior linemen such as Dylan Parham, Josh Myers and Joe Tippmann. With his ability to eat up blocks, he could play his way into a rotational role as a rookie.
“He’s long, he’s got big hands, he’s able to disengage and make a play,” Glenn said. “He can play gap-and-a-half, which I like between the defensive tackles. So, the more reps that he gets, I think the more comfortable he will get.”
The fifth-year tight end has been a pleasant surprise in the tight ends group, and rookie Kenyon Sadiq’s injury has allowed him more valuable reps with Smith and Klubnik. Sadiq suffered a setback in his return from offseason hernia surgery and is expected to miss some time.
As for Woods: He missed two full seasons with the Colts (2023 and 2024) because of injuries but is fully healthy and showing some of the potential that made him a second-round pick when offensive coordinator Frank Reich was the head coach in Indianapolis. He has some legitimate ability as a blocker and has made some impressive plays catching the ball, too. On Monday, he was targeted a handful of times and caught most of them.
“There’s a number of things that you can envision him doing for us,” Glenn said. “You can split him out and let him go one-on-one with a safety, a linebacker, and I’m expecting him to win that matchup.”

title: Carson Beck Says He's Ready for Biggest Test Yet With Arizona Cardinals
full_text:
GLENDALE — It's hard to surprise a player with as much experience as Carson Beck, but when the Arizona Cardinals informed him he'd be their starter for the NFL's Hall of Fame Game on Thursday, Beck was caught off guard.
"I had no clue that I was going to start," Beck told reporters. "Obviously, I thought I was going to play in it, but I really didn't have any expectations  going into any of this. Obviously our schedule is absolutely crazy right now. Practice meetings with training camp and whatnot, but yeah, I'm looking forward to it. I'm really excited."
Beck, a third-round pick this past April, is third in the pecking order behind Gardner Minshew and Jacoby Brissett — two players he says have been ultimate professionals towards him since landing in Arizona.
Thursday night won't win him the starting job, nor will it drastically alter the Cardinals' opinion of him — though it is an opportunity for Beck to step into a starting role on a national spotlight.
Beck's played in more big matchups than most third-round quarterbacks, leading both Miami and Georgia to respective appearances in national title games before entering the professional level.
Nerves haven't flared for Beck in quite some time.
"I think the last time I was nervous was when I was like eight years old, maybe for our like city championship, Pop Warner. It's just it's a game at the end of the day," said Beck.
"I get to go out there, have an opportunity to have fun, play with your teammates, and again play the game that I love."
Beck arrives to a Cardinals franchise that just ripped the band-aid off Kyler Murray after seven up-and-down years. Arizona's looking for their guy, and while a third-round rookie seldom fits that billing, there's hope Beck can prove himself as an outlier.
One step at a time, though. Before any thoughts of becoming an NFL legend occur, he first has to handle business in the mythical air of Canton.
"I think the biggest thing for me, especially just as we're going through training camp and we're still building the chemistry with the guys, is can we be on the same page as an offense?" said Beck when asked what will define a successful night.
"Are my eyes in the right spot? Am I making the right decisions? Am I making the right reads? Am I getting through my progressions quickly? I think that's success for us, and then ultimately getting in and out of the huddle and doing things the right way at a very high level."
Training camp thus far has been full of good and bad days, drives and reps for Beck. Cardinals offensive coordinator Nathaniel Hackett told reporters he's excited to see how Beck handles the ups and downs of an NFL game.
Beck believes he's done a good job of taking the good with the bad early in his career.
"I think these learning moments are so huge. Getting little things out of the way now is incredible and important but the more reps you get, the more comfortable you become, and you kind of start to understand what you're trying to accomplish," Beck said.
His biggest moment yet will come on Thursday.

title: Why I'm Buying the Carson Beck Hype as Cardinals' Hall of Fame Game Starter
full_text:
ARIZONA — The Arizona Cardinals finally made a call on who will be their starting quarterback during Thursday's Hall of Fame Game, and it's the right one.
Carson Beck is getting the nod, according to head coach Mike LaFleur. Beck, the third quarterback on Arizona's depth chart , will split time with Kedon Slovis as Jacoby Brissett and Gardner Minshew aren't expected to play against the Carolina Panthers.
The importance of Beck starting shouldn't be overblown or exaggerated. Beck's not going to win any starting jobs nor lose any faith from Cardinals brass over the course of his snaps in Canton.
With Arizona potentially eying a franchise quarterback next offseason, they'll need as much information as possible on Beck before making that decision, and Thursday's the biggest step thus far in that process.
Beck has strung together some strong performances in recent practices after starting out of the gates slower than some would have liked. That's life as a rookie quarterback, especially one taken in the third round, though it's been an overall mixed bag of performances.
"With any young player, I think there's always ups and downs," Cardinals offensive coordinator Nathaniel Hackett told reporters this week.
"You kind of expect that. I think he's had a couple really great days and a couple rough days, but again I think the thing that I really appreciate about him is he doesn't let it affect him. Some things might work, some things might not, but he's just going to try to take as much as he can from each one of those opportunities."
Beck's accuracy has been hit or miss depending on the day, though his arm talent has also been a highlight thus far.
There's something to be said about what the next step will entail for Beck, who will be getting his first taste of live competition at the NFL level. The proverbial bullets will be flying, and Beck will be tasked with elevating his game against players who aren't his own teammates.
"All of his experience. His age, his understanding that things are gonna go good and things are gonna go bad. Always understanding you can never get too excited, you can never get too frustrated because you're gonna have another play," Hackett highlighted on what he's seen from Beck.
"And the key was learning from those mistakes and growing from those, but I think Carson definitely has a very good command, and he's really excited about this opportunity."
The arm talent, pocket mobility and other various physical characteristics will be on display Thursday, though what makes starting Beck the correct call isn't what he does initially, but more so how he reacts.
Rookies make mistakes. Rookie quarterback mistakes are amplified and plastered across social media. We live in a world where time for development is essentially non-existent: either you're ready to save a franchise from the first day or you're just another brick in the wall of quarterbacks drafted.
Beck's extensive college experience made him an attractive piece for the Cardinals to target, both in hopes of immediately contributing in 2026 and beyond. With the available options in the third round, Beck's resume and profile was the obvious choice.
Yet anybody can look great in controlled environment, but how will Beck respond when adversity hits?
That's the selling point of why Thursday is a big day for the Miami/Georgia product.
"You can call a perfect play versus perfect coverage, and something can go wrong. There's a lot of people out there, a lot of human error that goes on in every single football play. And if it's good, again, we don't want him to get too excited. It's still a long game, and he'll have a lot of opportunity out there," Hackett continued.
"Anything that might [be] bad happens on an offensive football play, how do you respond the next play? If you lose yardage, you know are you excited about the opportunity next play, or are you thinking about that last one and letting it affect that next play? That's a huge mental part of our game, especially at that position."

title: Cardinals Finally Reveal Carson Beck Preseason Plan
full_text:
GLENDALE — It's officially a game week for the Arizona Cardinals.
The Cardinals are set to partake in the NFL's Hall of Fame Game this Thursday against the Carolina Panthers to officially kick off preseason festivities.
The Panthers have already named Kenny Pickett as their starting quarterback for Thursday, but we didn't know Arizona's plan — until now.
Head coach Mike LaFleur says Carson Beck will start.
Carson Beck will start at QB for the Cardinals in Thursday's Hall of Fame game, according to coach Mike LaFleur. pic.twitter.com/FGnYYv8892
Exactly how long Beck will play remains to be seen, though the Cardinals are likely not playing Jacoby Brissett or Gardner Minshew on Thursday – leaving it up to just Beck and Kedon Slovis to ring in the first preseason game of 2026.
Beck has had an up-and-down training camp so far. The Cardinals' rookie third-round pick struggled initially out of the gates but has picked up his performance in recent practices.
The Cardinals, with more than ten practices under their belt, prepare for an actual game this Thursday for the first time under LaFleur's watch.
"The guys that do play, it's their first time out there where coaches aren't you know right behind them or giving them a script," LaFleur said earlier this week.
"There is no script. We'll be tight with our plan. What I want to go see is these guys, their play style come to life, and us go operate before the snap. That's it. And then everything else is just those guys going out and letting it loose."
Most teams typically don't play their starters in their first preseason game, though there was intrigue in the desert with it being LaFleur's first season and the Cardinals having a fourth game on their schedule as opposed to the typical three.
"I don't want to overtalk it. It's a game, and again, when you put your body on the line, it's real live bullets out there. You got to mentally get yourself right, and it's not a problem as long as we approach it that way. And so we won't overtalk about it," LaFleur continued.
"It's just hey, 'we got to go play good football. We got to operate the right way, and our play style's got to come to life' and then when the ball snaps, you got to go execute. Sometimes it's going to be clean looks, and sometimes it's going to be a look that you've never seen, particularly in the preseason. Because it's not like we're watching film on Carolina, at all. Like we're not going to watch a snap of them.
"So we're just going to have a tight plan that is all inclusive for whatever they bring at us. Protected plays, if you will. You just want to see these guys come off the rock and go."
The Cardinals and Panthers square off in Canton, OH on Thursday, Aug. 6 at 5:00 PM Arizona time. The game will be broadcast on NBC.

title: Cardinals Get New Play-By-Play Voice
full_text:
ARIZONA — The Arizona Cardinals have a new play-by-play radio voice, as the organization announced J.P. Shadrick as the man to replace the legendary Dave Pasch.
More from the team's press release:
"Shadrick joins the Cardinals with more than 20 years of play-by-play experience in a wide range of sports, including NFL and college football, PGA Tour golf and minor league baseball.
"Nationally, he has called radio play-by-play for the NFL on Westwood One Sports since 2022, announcing NFL London games, Thanksgiving Day, Christmas Day and key late-season matchups. He has also served as a national play-by-play voice on college football for Touchdown Radio Network since 2017, with studio host experience since 2016.
"Shadrick has spent the last 14 seasons with the Jacksonville Jaguars as a senior reporter, hosting the last six Jaguars head coaches’ weekly radio shows while serving as a pregame and postgame radio host on gameday. He also contributed to Jaguars Television Network shows while anchoring Jaguars.com coverage of free agency, the NFL Draft and other major offseason events.
"Originally from Trussville, AL, Shadrick graduated from the University of Alabama in 2004."
The Cardinals' radio booth has seen massive changes within the last few years, seeing legends such as Pasch and color commentator Ron Wolfley step away. Shadrick will join A.Q. Shipley in the booth to form what many hope to be a formidable tandem moving into the future.
"Shadrick will make his Cardinals radio debut on Thursday, August 13 when Arizona travels to Las Vegas to take on the Raiders in a 5:00 PM game from Allegiant Stadium. All Cardinals games can be heard on Arizona Sports 98.7 FM," the press release continues.
"In addition to calling the games, Shadrick will contribute to various Cardinals broadcast programming and events throughout the year."
Dani Sureck is still on the sideline as a reporter.
"Dave Pasch is one of the great voices in our game and I appreciate the high standard that he left behind," Shadrick said to AZCardinals.com .
"I'm eager to work toward matching that but also take it further in my own style. I'm fired up to work with A.Q. Shipley too, his great personality combined with his in-depth knowledge of the game in all aspects makes him a top-tier analyst."

title: Arizona Cardinals HC Has Three-Word Answer on Josh Sweat's Week 1 Status
full_text:
GLENDALE — Josh Sweat has yet to make an appearance for the Arizona Cardinals in 2026.
That dates back to offseason team activities, where he wasn't present before he was on the sidelines for mandatory minicamp. At the beginning of training camp, the Cardinals placed him on PUP, and he's yet to come off the list.
He hasn't been spotted on the sidelines during practice, either.
Sweat doesn't appear likely to play in the preseason, and as speculation swirls around what exactly is happening with Arizona's top pass rusher, the Cardinals are confident he'll be ready for the regular season.
"I do. Yes," said head coach Mike LaFleur when asked if he'll be ready for Week 1.
Sweat has been a consistent topic surrounding the Cardinals despite not being on the field after early reports of a trade request this offseason. LaFleur, asked earlier in camp on Sweat , insisted there was no discontent on his end before adding:
"He's always stayed away in those phase one, phase two, phase three [periods]. He was working with our team pretty good. And he was around. That's what Josh has done, and that's what's worked for Josh to get himself in position to play the best football, and we knew that. Not that I was here a year ago, but we knew that when we brought him in. I knew that when I first got here in February.
"So the cool part about Josh is everyone's been on the same page the entire time. You guys can believe me or not, I'm not worried about Josh Sweat at all in terms of his health and all that. [He needs] a little bit more time, he's logged a lot of miles in this league as well. I think not only for Josh to peak on September 13, but Josh to also get through the rigors of a 17-game season the way that he plays and the motor that he plays with, I think this is best for him and the Cardinals."
Sweat's 12 sacks last season were nearly double of the second-highest Cardinals player in Calais Campbell (6.5), who is no longer with the team. The next-highest individual totals were two sacks each from Baron Browning and Walter Nolen III.
Sweat's presence within Arizona's defense is vital for the Cardinals entering the 2026 season, as the team made virtually zero improvements to its pass rush over the course of the offseason.

title: Trey Benson Trade Buzz Growing Louder After Cardinals Roster Moves
full_text:
GLENDALE — Trade buzz continues to heighten around over Arizona Cardinals running back Trey Benson.
Benson was not spotted at yesterday's practice — not even dressed on the sideline — and head coach Mike LaFleur (who is pretty good at keeping reporters updated via injury) didn't mention his potential absence ahead of Sunday's practice.
There was already trade speculation around Benson entering his third season in the league, though his absence yesterday was followed today by the Cardinals claiming running back Evan Hull while working out fellow ball-carrier Jermar Jefferson, which only ignited that speculation.
The #AZCardinals waived DL Coziah Izzard and WR Tejhaun Palmer and claimed DT Cam Horsley and RB Evan Hull. Cardinals also tried out RB Jermar Jefferson. Notable since RB Trey Benson was not spotted at practice yesterday
LaFleur says his absence was due to injury:
"Just a little discomfort, little flare up in the left knee. It's unfortunate because he was feeling so good, and I thought he was really getting his legs underneath him. I thought he strung together some good days. It was good news today that he was feeling much better," he told reporters ahead of Monday.
Benson has been an obvious trade candidate for the Cardinals since the arrival of Tyler Allgeier (free agency) and Jeremiyah Love (draft) — on top of James Conner, who restructured his contract to stay with the team for 2026.
A former Day 2 draft pick, Benson's early career in Arizona has been marked by injuries and inconsistent opportunity/play. He's shown the ability to pop off a big run, similar to his days at Florida State, though he's yet to realize his full potential in the Cardinals' backfield.
The Cardinals seem intent on running the ball plenty, though with such a top heavy backfield in Allgeier/Love/Conner, Benson is very much on the outside looking in.
He was named a loser in our winners/losers of training camp so far, which you can find here .
Not only has Benson's role in Arizona's offense taken a hit — his chances of being on the roster have as well. Benson was listed as RB4 on the Cardinals' first depth chart, though Bam Knight has seen more team work ahead of Benson as we enter Arizona's first preseason game.
Knight very well could get a final nod thanks to special teams work if a decision comes down between the two of them. Benson has seen limited action during 11 v 11 opportunities, and when he has participated, it's been with the third team.
The Cardinals, in an ideal world, would trade Benson before cutting him for a late-round pick. There's plenty of running back-needy teams who would send a flyer to get Benson, who simply might need a change of scenery to thrive.
Benson has played 17 games for the Cardinals across his two NFL seasons. He ended on injured reserve both seasons with an ankle (2024) and knee (2025) injuries. On 92 rushes he's averaged 4.9 yards per carry with one touchdown to his name.
